text: Welcome to lesson nineteen. Drift checks look at inputs. Performance monitoring looks at what matters most: is the model still right?

Monitor in layers. Input drift checks fire first, because they need no labels. Then outcome metrics follow as labels arrive. Track a ranking metric like A U C, the metric the business acts on, such as precision in the top twenty percent, and calibration, meaning predicted rates against actual rates. Finally, route alerts by severity: warnings to a channel, critical problems to a person.

Here is a weekly report from eight simulated weeks of the churn model. Input drift starts in week three, and P S I jumps, but A U C only wobbles. Concept drift creeps in from week five, and A U C slides to point four five by week eight, while top-twenty-percent precision falls from point three one to point zero three seven. Remember, real labels arrive late, so each real report lags by your label delay.

Set thresholds from the training baseline. The baseline A U C was point seven four four, so the critical floor is that minus point zero five, or point six nine four. Add a calibration gap limit of point zero three, and the P S I limit of point two five. A U C below the floor is critical. The other two are warnings.
The dashboard shows it plainly. A U C crosses the alert floor in week five and keeps falling, and the actual cancel rate drifts away from the predicted rate.

One bad week can be noise. With about one hundred sixty five cancellations a week, week five's confidence interval straddles the floor. So require two breaches in a row before paging anyone. The breach weeks are five through eight, but the paging weeks are six through eight. That one extra week of patience removes the shaky first alert and protects your team from alert fatigue.
